summary:
What we developed. SELENE is a web application that lets mission planners, educators and the public explore lunar landing regions and compare dates. For a chosen site and time window it shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the local terrain horizon, using an interactive 3D Moon, a regional terrain view built from NASA LOLA heights, a 360° skyline and a mission timeline. It also reports sunlight per window, direct Earth view and the longest Sun blockage.

How it addresses the challenge. It turns complex ephemeris and topography data from JPL Horizons, LOLA and LROC into clear, comparable views, so users can assess solar-power potential and direct-to-Earth communication without navigating several specialist tools. Several regions, including Shackleton, Malapert and de Gerlache, can be compared over the same window, and users can enter custom coordinates.

Why it matters. Near the lunar south pole, small changes in site or date can strongly change power and communication conditions. SELENE helps teams re-check options quickly when a mission slips. It is transparent: if a NASA source is unavailable, results are shown as unavailable, and its limitations are stated openly.
details:
What it does and how it works. SELENE lets users pick a lunar region or enter custom coordinates, choose a start date and a window (7 days or one lunar day), and see whether the Sun and Earth clear the local terrain horizon. It samples NASA LOLA heights (0.25° grid) to build a 360° skyline (1° azimuth steps, 2 km distance steps, 8 to 150 km range, spherical curvature, 2 m observer height). It requests Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation from JPL Horizons (airless, 2-hour steps, angles interpolated) and compares each body with the skyline over 240 samples. Outputs are sunlight per window, direct Earth view, longest Sun blockage, a timeline, a regional 3D terrain view (about 160 km, vertical relief ×4) and an exportable snapshot.

Benefits and intended impact. Mission planners, educators and the public can compare regions such as Shackleton, Malapert, de Gerlache and Apollo 11 over the same window in one interface, instead of switching between several specialist tools. The goal is faster re-checking when a mission’s site or date changes.

Tools. JavaScript (ES modules), HTML/CSS, Canvas and WebGL; Node.js 22 for the dev server, build and tests; a server function that proxies JPL Horizons; GitHub for the source [and Netlify for hosting]. Data: JPL Horizons, LOLA elevation and LROC colour texture (NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit). Fonts: DM Sans and Space Grotesk. AI assistance: OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex and Claude for research, interface design, code and tests. No special hardware.

Creativity. The app is framed as a question (“Where would you land?”) with a guided mission, an interactive 3D Moon, a terrain view and a mission clock, in English and Russian.

Factors considered. The Moon has no atmosphere, so no refraction is applied. Terrain inside 8 km is unresolved, and the tool is a regional screening aid, not a landing-safety certification. It is not flight-validated and does not model finite disks, eclipses or detailed shadows. We never substitute invented data: if a NASA source is unavailable, dependent results show as unavailable.
